This web service provides three main functionalities: (1) Transcriptomics in snRNA-seq data, which illustrates gene expression on UMAP and cell type grouping; (2) Epigenomics in snATAC-seq data, which shows peak accessibility, linkage, and motif information; (3) Spatial omics of multiome data, which includes gene, peak, cell type, gene set, and peak set enrichment visualized on a corn plot. ST-MAGIC enables users to explore spatial and temporal patterns in a user-friendly manner. For transcriptomics, profiled genes can be searched for their expression patterns over space and time. For epigenomics, profiled peaks and motifs can be used to investigate spatial and temporal accessibility patterns. In addition, ST-MAGIC provides a selection list of gene sets or peak sets from SCENIC+ to TF enrichment analysis.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In “Spatiotemporal Regulatory Logics of Mouse Gastrulation”, Yang et al describe two resources, ST-MAGIC and ST-MAGIC+, that project new single cell multimodal transcriptome and ATAC-seq data collected for 4 timepoints between E6.5-E7.5 during mouse gastrulation onto the published Geo-seq spatial profiling atlas. To identify gene regulatory networks, the authors introduce a new software package, BioCRE, to analyze multimodal transcriptome information with ATAC-seq data to link genes with accessibility peaks. The authors describe several vignettes including dissection of the GRNs and enhancers that guide mesendoderm development to showcase how these resources can be used. Through those vignettes, they identify novel enhancer elements and transcription factors that may affect differentiation.

The manuscript is a tour-de-force work integrating many published data sets and tools. Indeed, most figures both in the main text and supplementary had a very large number of panels. The manuscript was reasonably well written so that I could follow the logic through analysis of this complex data set and I commend the authors for providing many data panels. The schematics as the first panel for several figures was helpful. Moreover, I appreciated the generation of new data to follow up new hypotheses (Pou6f1 KO and Noto KO multi-seq data) and the RNA-scope experiments for validation.

Nonetheless, it was difficult to assess many of the claims due to a lack of quantification, statistical tests, and useful visualizations. While the development of new analysis platforms like BioCRE is useful, BioCRE was not adequately benchmarked against other methods and so it is difficult to evaluate its contribution to this manuscript.

General comments:
I recommend a different title for this manuscript as the current one suggests more comprehensive profiling across time.
The legend captions should be more descriptive and explain nomenclature used in the figure. For example, I think peaks are often shortened to “p” and genes are often shortened to “g”.

Point-by-point comments sectioned by the main figure referenced:
Figure 1
ED Fig 1a: The quality of the E6.75 data set looks poor compared to the other data sets (notably fewer genes and UMIs detected, more mitochondrial RNA). While I believe the majority of the vignettes presented in the manuscript rely on the later timepoints, the utility of this data set as a resource would require that the data is of high quality. Is it possible that the lower quality is reflective of biology or was there noticeable difference in sample quality or preparation for the E6.75 data set?
Lines 114-116: Please include the number of embryos pooled for each time point.
ED Fig 1g: What method was used to count approx. cell numbers of embryos? A table highlighting the number of cells per embryo per timepoint would be useful to give a sense of embryo staging.
ED Fig 3a: Please add details to the legend. How are the values computed? Is it the cluster compared against the rest of the cells? Does the colorbar refer to log2 fold change?
Lines 154-165: There is not enough analysis benchmarking BioCRE against Signac and ArchR. What other metrics can be used to measure the consistency of gene expression and peaks? What are the set characteristics between the linkage predictions of the three tools (does BioCRE identify a super set of linkage? Are many predictions non-overlapping?). What are the run-time characteristics for BioCRE compared to the other tools? How does sampling affect BioCRE performance? Example: downsample the RNA-seq and ATAC-seq together, down-sample one while holding the other constant, etc. How does the median gene-to-peak distance compare between methods?
Figure 2
ED Fig 4b: There is a general trend of increasing JSD score with timepoint. Can the authors speculate why? Is it due to the number of cell types?
ED Fig 4d: The claim is that the expression of Sox2 closely matches between the GEO-seq data and ST-MAGIC gene expression. This is hard to evaluate from the figure panel. A scatter plot would aid evaluation of the claim. Moreover, the proposed visualization can be done for all genes and provide a better measurement to understand the similarity between GEO-seq and ST-MAGIC.
Fig 2g and h: The schematic is not useful.
Lines 272-274: Are the differences statistically significant?
ED Fig 6g: How many gastruloids where generated and measured in this experiment? Did the authors observe morphological differences between the cell lines or different generation efficiencies?
Figure 3
Lines 307-308: How were Etv2, Gata2 and Tal1 selected from the SCENIC+ candidates? Do the other TF candidates that fit the TF expression hierarchy display the same paradigm of the upstream factor functioning as a priming factor responsible for opening chromatin for use by later factors?
Lines 342-346: How many target genes and target peaks are there for NOTO?
Fig 3e: It is difficult to evaluate the claim that target genes of NOTO and NOTO expression have matched spatiotemporal distribution with the provided visualization. Moreover, the authors should leverage their comprehensive integrated atlas, to evaluate how many genes and their targets nominated by SCENIC+ display similar behavior. It is not clear why Noto is selected from the candidates SCENIC+ nominates for mesendoderm development. It does not appear to be highlighted in ED Fig 7.
Figure 4
Lines 374-380: There are claims about the specific and global spatial expression patterns for different factors. While these assessments can be made by eye using the overlay onto the spatial coordinates, a quantitative assessment is more valuable. For example, if the authors plot a histogram of the values for each spot, the factors that show specific expression patterns and those that are global will be obvious. To be clear, I think both the plots the authors provide and the quantifications I recommend are needed.
Fig 4b,c: The claim is that Wnt3 and Dkk1 have overlapping distributions. This is difficult to assess by the provided panels. Moreover, can any statistics be applied to this analysis? Are the peaks enriched?
Figure 5
Lines 463-466: There is not a figure panel that shows the co-expression pattern for Shh, Noto, and Foxj1. I believe Fig 5e might be the panel but it does not have Shh or Noto highlighted. It is difficult to assess the claim that these two distinct subtypes exist.
Line 514: What does a “highly specific distribution” mean for POU6F1? Can the authors support this claim with a statistic?
Figure 6
Line 531: “The target genes start to show abundant enrichment at the same region”. From inspection of Fig 6a, it appears to me that the POU6F1 target gene set expression appears before the expression of Pou6f1 with the former appearing at E7.25. Can the authors explain the differential timing of these events?
Lines 532-535: The authors suggest that “early and intermediate stage TFs may function as priming factors by opening a broad range of chromatin regions”. This is a reasonable hypothetical model. Can the authors support or refute this claim with additional analysis? For example, are the target peaks from early and intermediate stage TFs enriched for terminal TF targets? From Fig 5m,n, the number of peaks and genes targeted by Eomes (42p, 35g respectively) is far less than the number of peaks and genes targeted by Pou6f1 (127p, 99g respectively). It's not clear to me how to incorporate these numbers into the proposed model.
Lines 547-551, Fig 6c: The authors described that EOMES and FOXA2 ChIP-seq data shows enrichment of these TFs around the peaks of NOTO and POU6F1 targets. First, the text does not describe the ChIP-seq data. The citations are in the legend and only by looking at the papers could I discern what the ChIP-seq data is, which is from EBs and in vitro differentiation, respectively I believe. Second, there is no statistical test for the enrichment but I agree that by eye, there is a peak for both Eomes and FoxA2. However, it does not appear from the data presented in Fig 6c that the Eomes KO has an effect on these peaks implying that the chromatin regulation may be controlled by other factors. I would agree that F2-KO does have an effect but does not entirely explain the regulation at those target loci. Will the authors please explain or modify the following statement in the text: “EOMES and FOXA2 are likely to be responsible for pre-opening… target chromatin regions”.
Minor points:
Fig 1e: I believe JSD index is incorrect. JSD measures the similarity between two distributions. The Jensen-Shannon diversity index is a special case of JSD.
ED Fig 1g: needs a color legend for cell types
ED Fig 2b: The text describes cell types that are enriched at earlier or later time points. To aid this visual assessment, it would be helpful if the x-axis had the same scale for each time point.
ED Fig 3h: units on y axis. How many replicates per condition?
ED Fig 10e: Needs a summary plot at the top of the heatmap such as in Fig 2i.
Line 486: It is not clear what Combinatorial pseudo-time based tracking means.
ED Fig 12f: Caption missing explanation of acronyms in panel (EB – embryoid body, MEN - ?)
Line 569, ED Fig 13h: I realize the numbers are small, but it would nonetheless be useful for the authors to derive a likelihood (p-value) for the axis turning randomization.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript, Yang and colleagues present a spatiotemporal dataset capturing mouse gastrulation, generated using 10x Genomics Multiome data. The study involves a significant amount of data integration and projection, incorporating external datasets such as Geo-seq and ChIP-seq. To enable gene regulatory network (GRN) analysis, the authors developed a new computational tool called BioCREs, which they claim performs better than existing pipelines. They also adapted the Tangram algorithm—originally designed for high-resolution spatial transcriptomics—for use with their data to align it with Geo-seq references. Through this combined approach, they aim to map spatial and temporal regulatory changes during gastrulation.

The scope of this work is impressive, and the integration of multiple data types is interesting. The authors also acknowledge the limitations of current spatial resolution and mismatched cell type references, which are important caveats. I appreciate the validation experiments included, which lend support to some of their conclusions. That said, I do have several concerns, especially regarding the BioCREs pipeline and the modified Tangram tool.

Major Concerns:
1. The claim that BioCREs outperforms Signac and ArchR is based on a single performance index. This is insufficient to justify the claim. Benchmarking against established regulatory element datasets (e.g., ENCODE) is necessary to validate accuracy and specificity.
2. Distal vs. Proximal regulatory region comparison: The comparison between "Distal High" and "Proximal" groups is biased by excluding the "Distal Low" group. A more appropriate comparison would be between all distal regions and proximal ones, with proper statistical testing (e.g., p-values) to support conclusions.
3. Insufficient benchmarking for BioCREs and modified Tangram: The manuscript lacks technical detail and performance benchmarking for both pipelines. More rigorous testing is needed to demonstrate their robustness and reliability.
4. Incorporating data from high-resolution platforms such as Visium HD or Stereo-seq would significantly strengthen the spatial claims. Even one matching experiment would add credibility.

Minor Comments:
• The manuscript is dense, especially in later sections discussing biological processes. Streamlining these parts would improve accessibility.
• Some extended data figures are poorly organized and should be revised for clarity.
• Clarity in Extended Data Fig. 2a: The plot is overcrowded due to overlapping cells, making it difficult to interpret. A side-by-side comparison with reference data in separate panels would improve readability.
• Missing data in Extended Fig. 4: The claim that ST-MAGIC has higher JSD values than Geo-seq is not supported by the figure. This should be clarified or removed.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Responses to Reviewers
Summary of major new data
We would like to thank the reviewers for their valuable input. We provide a revised version
of the manuscript with a substantial body of new analyses and experiment data that further
confirm and strengthen the conclusions. Please note that we used Fig. 1, 2, 3, etc. to refer
to figures in the revised manuscript and Response Fig. R1, R2, R3, etc. to refer to figures
in this letter.
1. We systematically benchmarked the performance of BioCRE through evaluating the
biological relevance, cell type specificity of gene-to-peak linkages, the computational
efficiency, and consistency of linkage composition under various sample sizes. Moreover,
through using publicly available single-cell multiome and matched promoter-capture HiC
datasets, we identified the reliability and accuracy of linkage prediction. These analyses
collectively demonstrated that BioCRE outperforms Signac and BioCRE in predicting
reliable and accurate gene-to-peak linkages.
2. We compared the ST-MAGIC atlas with a high-resolution Stereo-seq dataset (SEU-3D)
for E7.5 embryo. As demonstrated by analyzing cell type-specific transcriptomic
architectures, signature gene set distributions, spatial locations of cell types and gene
expression patterns, ST-MAGIC shows high spatial consistency with SEU-3D. Furthermore,
in-depth evaluation highlighted the effective attributes of ST-MAGIC in detecting low-
abundance genes.
3. We incorporated additional metrics (such as Pearson correlation, structural similarity
index, P-value) and versatile plots (histogram, scatter plot, density plot) to quantitatively
evaluate the global similarities between ST-MAGIC and Geo-seq atlas, and
comprehensively assessed the spatiotemporal relationships for distinct signal cascades
and eRegulons. Overall, the original spatial claims have been substantially strengthened.
4. We conducted additional gastruloid differentiation experiments to determine the roles of
Neo_LRE element and collected more mutant embryos to summarize the phenotypic
significances for Noto mutant and Pou6f1 mutant embryos. Consequently, we
demonstrated the roles of Neo_LRE in regulating Lefty2 expression, and confirmed the
axis turning defects of Noto mutant and Pou6f1 mutant embryos.

ED Fig 3a: Please add details to the legend. How are the values computed? Is it the cluster

Response: Thank you for these comments. We apologize for the lack of clarity regarding the
details of this figure. To clarify, the values are scaled transformations of the original raw data
and do not represent cluster-versus-rest comparisons or log2 fold changes. Specifically, for the
gene expression heatmap, the values are scaled results derived from gene count data, adjusted

Lines 154-165: There is not enough analysis benchmarking BioCRE against Signac and ArchR.
What other metrics can be used to measure the consistency of gene expression and peaks?
What are the set characteristics between the linkage predictions of the three tools (does
BioCRE identify a super set of linkage? Are many predictions non-overlapping?). What are the
run-time characteristics for BioCRE compared to the other tools? How does sampling affect
BioCRE performance? Example: downsample the RNA-seq and ATAC-seq together, down-
sample one while holding the other constant, etc. How does the median gene-to-peak distance
compare between methods?
Response: Thanks for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree that a more comprehensive
benchmarking strategy is essential to substantiate our claim that BioCRE outperforms existing
tools.
In this revision, to benchmark the performance of BioCRE, we have conducted a series of
systematic evaluations to rigorously compare the performance of BioCRE against the state-of-
the-art methods: Signac and ArchR.
1. The characteristics of predicted gene-to-peak linkages:
Using our multi-omic dataset from the mouse gastrula, we evaluated the number, biological
relevance, and cell type specificity of predicted gene-to-peak linkages. As shown, BioCRE
identified 44,644 gene-to-peak linkages, with a median gene-to-peak distance of 127,175 bp
(Response Fig. R3a, b). Comparative analyses revealed that 28,472 linkages (64%) were
specifically identified in BioCRE (Response Fig. R3c, d). Gene ontology analyses of genes
associated with these BioCRE-specific linkages (28,472 linkages) revealed significant
enrichment in embryo development, including heart development, liver development, and
nervous system development (Response Fig. R3e). This result suggests that these BioCRE-
specific linkages could be responsible for the regulation of embryo development related genes.
To assess the cell type specificity of predicted linkages, we analyzed the accessibility of peaks
linked to cell type-specific genes identified by each tool (Response Fig. R3f, g). Using UMAP
visualization and quantifying clustering coherence with the Silhouette score, we found that
linkages predicted by BioCRE gets a higher score compared to those from Signac and ArchR,
indicating a more effective capability for BioCRE to capture cell type-specific linkages
(Response Fig. R3f, g).
Together, these results demonstrate that BioCRE could be adept at identify cell type-specific
linkages, which are likely to play key roles in orchestrating embryo development.
2. The computational efficiency and robustness for predicting linkages:
We assessed the computational efficiency and robustness of different methods under varying
sampling conditions. Overall, we found that the built-in deep-learning bi-orientation regression
model for BioCRE does not incur excessive run-time costs, showing comparable performance
to ArchR (Response Fig. R3h). To evaluate the robustness of linkage identification, we
checked the consistency of predicted linkages across three distinct down-sampling scenarios:
 In the first scenario, where both RNA and peak reads were down-sampled concurrently,
BioCRE demonstrated the highest recovery rate of linkage identification (Response Fig.
R3i). To specify, 40.9% linkages (31,911 out of 78,109) are constantly identified in BioCRE,
while only 8.2% linkages (3,677 out of 44,705) for Signac and 5.7% linkages (4,479 out of
79,067) for ArchR show consistent results among variable sample sizes (Response Fig.
R3i-1).
 In the second scenario, where only RNA reads were down-sampled while peak reads
remain unchanged, we found that 44.6% linkages (21,406 out of 48,043) are consistently
captured for BioCRE (Response Fig. R3i-2). In the meantime, 42.9% linkages (18,335
out of 42,937) for Signac and 61.9% linkages (38,510 out of 62,226) for ArchR are stably
identified (Response Fig. R3i-2).
 In the last scenario, we specifically down-sampled peak reads and then performed linkage
identification (Response Fig. R3i-3). Consequently, we found that 52.1% linkages
(49,476/95,042) for BioCRE are captured across all down-sampling groups (Response
Fig. R3i-3). In contrast, only 24.1% linkages (9,122/37,894) for Signac and 46.2% linkages
(28,388/61,422) for ArchR show the same pattern (Response Fig. R3i-3).
Collectively, these analyses demonstrate that BioCRE achieves a favorable balance between
computational efficiency and robustness, exhibiting consistency and high reproducibility in
linkage prediction across diverse and reduced sequencing depths—particularly under
conditions of limited chromatin accessibility data (Scenario 1 and 3)—highlighting its reliability
in practical, resource-variable settings.
3. The reliability and accuracy of predicted linkages:
Given the absence of a genome-wide gold standard for gene-to-peak linkages in the mouse
gastrula, we turned to external single-cell multiome datasets with matched, high-confidence
promoter-enhancer interaction data to benchmark performance. Specifically, we applied
BioCRE, Signac and ArchR to publicly available single-cell multiome data from human PBMC
cells and Gm12878 cells, using promoter-capture Hi-C (PCHiC) data as an orthogonal
reference for true regulatory interactions (Response Fig. R3j).
To enable a comprehensive and balanced evaluation, we defined both positive and negative
controls: positive linkages were inferred from PCHiC-confirmed interactions, while negative
linkages were established as peak-gene pairs showing no chromatin interactions within a 1 Mb
range in the PCHiC data. We evaluated the performance using multiple following metrics:
 The metrics of Macro-F1 score across all linkages showed that BioCRE consistently
achieved higher scores than both Signac and ArchR across all tested cell types, with strong
reproducibility across replicates (Response Fig. R3j-1). This indicates that BioCRE’s
predictions more closely align with the experimentally determined chromatin architecture.
 The Macro-F1 score for linkages of all three tools shared genes revealed that BioCRE
outperformed both Signac and ArchR in most cell types, where its advantage was less
pronounced (Response Fig. R3j-2).
 The True Positive Rate (TPR) for linkages unique to each method was also assessed.
BioCRE-specific linkages show comparable or higher level of TPR than those of Signac
and ArchR (Response Fig. R3j-3), suggesting that BioCRE-specific predictions are not
only robust but also biologically credible.
Thus, through incorporating external dataset and gold standard chromatin interaction dataset,
we demonstrated that BioCRE exhibits consistent superiority in linkage identification than
Signac and ArchR.
These results have been included in the revised manuscript (Line 162-176; Supplementary
Fig. 4), the detailed method has been provided in Line 982-1038, and we also acknowledged
the significance of systematically benchmark of BioCRE performance and discussed about the
current limitations in Line 623-632, Line 703-705.
Response Figure R3. Benchmark of BioCRE. a. Bar plot showing the number of gene-peak linkages identified by
BioCRE, Signac, and ArchR, respectively. b. Histogram showing the gene-peak distance for linkages identified by
BioCRE, Signac, and ArchR, respectively. c. Venn diagram showing the intersection of predicted gene-peak linkages.
d. Bar plot highlighting the ratio of non-overlapping linkage ratios for each tool. e. Gene ontology analyses for BioCRE-
specific captured linkages associated genes. f. UMAP plot based on the chromatin accessibility of cell type-specific
genes associated peaks. g. Silhouette score evaluating the cell type distribution specificity. h. Line plot depicting the
runtime for each tool with variable proportion of reads. BioCRE was running on a single GPU (A100), while ArchR and
Signac were executed using 20 CPU cores for parallel computing, respectively. i. The effects of sequencing reads
down-sampling on linkage composition consistency for each tool. The constant linkage numbers for each scenario were
highlighted in red. j. The prediction and validation of gene-peak linkages using external multiome dataset and gold
standard promoter-enhancer interaction dataset.

The current SCENIC+ pipeline starts with identifying candidate enhancers from 10xscMultiome-
snATAC-seq dataset. The scATAC-seq results can only capture a certain portion of
representative targets due to data sparsity. Given this, towards comprehensive analyses of the
relationship between early/intermediate and late TFs, we used the ChIP-seq dataset to explore
the relationship between early/intermediate and late stage TFs. In this study, using the
published dataset for early/intermediate (EOMES/FOXA2) factor from in vitro differentiation

other co-factors, thus facilitating the terminal binding and functioning of terminal stage TFs9,10.

other proteins, including ATP-dependent chromatin remodeler-SWI/SNF, to enable further
chromatin opening by late stage TFs (Response Fig. R17e)11,12. Thus, the target peaks of
pioneer factors (early/intermediate) are not necessarily larger than those of late-acting factors.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, Yang and colleagues present a spatiotemporal dataset capturing mouse
gastrulation, generated using 10x Genomics Multiome data. The study involves a
significant amount of data integration and projection, incorporating external datasets such
as Geo-seq and ChIP-seq. To enable gene regulatory network (GRN) analysis, the authors
developed a new computational tool called BioCREs, which they claim performs better
than existing pipelines. They also adapted the Tangram algorithm—originally designed for
high-resolution spatial transcriptomics—for use with their data to align it with Geo-seq
references. Through this combined approach, they aim to map spatial and temporal
regulatory changes during gastrulation.
The scope of this work is impressive, and the integration of multiple data types is interesting.
The authors also acknowledge the limitations of current spatial resolution and mismatched
cell type references, which are important caveats. I appreciate the validation experiments
included, which lend support to some of their conclusions. That said, I do have several
concerns, especially regarding the BioCREs pipeline and the modified Tangram tool.
Response: We highly appreciate the reviewer’s positive assessment and constructive
suggestions on our manuscript. In this revision, we have carefully revised the manuscript,
especially for the benchmarking of BioCRE pipeline and comparing the ST-MAGIC results with
Stereo-seq results. Generally, these efforts further strengthen our results.
Major Concerns:
1. The claim that BioCREs outperforms Signac and ArchR is based on a single
performance index. This is insufficient to justify the claim. Benchmarking against
established regulatory element datasets (e.g., ENCODE) is necessary to validate accuracy
and specificity.
Response: Thanks for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree that a more comprehensive
benchmarking strategy is essential to substantiate our claim that BioCRE outperforms existing
tools.
In this revision, to systematically benchmark the performance of BioCRE, we have conducted
a series of systematic evaluations to rigorously compare the performance of BioCRE against
the state-of-the-art methods: Signac and ArchR.
1. The set characteristics of predicted gene-to-peak linkages:
Using our multi-omic dataset from the mouse gastrula, we evaluated the number, biological
relevance, and cell type specificity of predicted gene-to-peak linkages. As shown, BioCRE
identified 44,644 gene-to-peak linkages, with a median gene-to-peak distance of 127,175 bp
(Response Fig. R23a, b). Comparative analyses revealed that 28,472 linkages (64%) were
specifically identified in BioCRE (Response Fig. R23c, d). Gene ontology analyses of genes
associated with these BioCRE-specific linkages (28,472 linkages) revealed significant
enrichment in embryo development, including heart development, liver development, and
nervous system development (Response Fig. R23e). This result suggests that these BioCRE-
specific linkages could be responsible for the regulation of embryo development related genes.
To assess the cell type specificity of predicted linkages, we analyzed the accessibility of peaks
linked to cell type-specific genes identified by each tool (Response Fig. R23f, g). Using UMAP
visualization and quantifying clustering coherence with the Silhouette score, we found that
linkages predicted by BioCRE gets a higher score compared to those from Signac and ArchR,
indicating a more effective capability for BioCRE to capture cell type-specific linkages
(Response Fig. R23f, g).
Together, these results demonstrate that BioCRE could be adept at identify cell-type-specific
linkages, which are likely to play key roles in orchestrating embryo development.
2. The computational efficiency and robustness of predicting linkages:
We assessed the computational efficiency and robustness of different methods under varying
sampling conditions. Overall, we found that the built-in deep-learning bi-orientation regression
model for BioCRE does not incur excessive run-time costs, showing comparable performance
to ArchR (Response Fig. R23h). To evaluate the robustness of linkage identification, we
checked the consistency of predicted linkages across three distinct down-sampling scenarios:
 In the first scenario, where both RNA and peak reads were down-sampled concurrently,
BioCRE demonstrated the highest recovery rate of linkage identification (Response Fig.
R23i). To specify, 40.9% linkages (31,911 out of 78,109) are constantly identified in
BioCRE, while only 8.2% linkages (3,677 out of 44,705) for Signac and 5.7% linkages
(4,479 out of 79,067) for ArchR show consistent results among variable sample sizes
(Response Fig. R23i-1).
 In the second scenario, where only RNA reads were down-sampled while peak reads
remain unchanged, we found that 44.6% linkages (21,406 out of 48,043) are consistently
captured for BioCRE (Response Fig. R23i-2). In the meantime, 42.9% linkages (18,335
out of 42,937) for Signac and 61.9% linkages (38,510 out of 62,226) for ArchR are stably
identified (Response Fig. R23i-2).
 In the last scenario, we specifically down-sampled peak reads and then performed linkage
identification (Response Fig. R23i-3). Consequently, we found that 52.1% linkages
(49,476/95,042) for BioCRE are captured across all down-sampling groups (Response
Fig. R23i-3). In contrast, only 24.1% linkages (9,122/37,894) for Signac and 46.2%
linkages (28,388/61,422) for ArchR show the same pattern (Response Fig. R23i-3).
Collectively, these analyses demonstrate that BioCRE achieves a favorable balance between
computational efficiency and robustness, exhibiting consistently high reproducibility in linkage
prediction across diverse and reduced sequencing depths, particularly under conditions of
limited chromatin accessibility data (Scenario 1 and 3), highlighting its reliability in practical,
resource-variable setting.
3. The reliability and accuracy of gene-to-peak linkages:
Given the absence of a genome-wide gold standard for gene-to-peak linkages in the mouse
gastrula, we turned to external single-cell multiome datasets with matched, high-confidence
promoter-enhancer interaction data to benchmark performance. Specifically, we applied
BioCRE, Signac and ArchR to publicly available single-cell multiome data from human PBMC
cells and Gm12878 cells, using promoter-capture Hi-C (PCHiC) data as an orthogonal
reference for true regulatory interactions (Response Fig. R23j).
To enable a comprehensive and balanced evaluation, we defined both positive and negative
controls: positive linkages were inferred from PCHiC-confirmed interactions, while negative
linkages were established as peak-gene pairs showing no chromatin interactions within a 1 Mb
range in the PCHiC data. We evaluated the performance using multiple following metrics:
 The metrics of Macro-F1 score across all linkages showed that BioCRE consistently
achieved higher scores than both Signac and ArchR across all tested cell types, with strong
reproducibility across replicates (Response Fig. R23j-1). This indicates that BioCRE’s
predictions more closely align with the experimentally determined chromatin architecture.
 The Macro-F1 score for linkages of all three tools shared genes revealed that BioCRE
outperformed both Signac and ArchR in most cell types except in CD16 monocyte, , where
its advantage was less pronounced (Response Fig. R23j-2).
 The True Positive Rate (TPR) for linkages unique to each method was also assessed.
BioCRE-specific linkages show comparable or higher level of TPR than those of Signac
and ArchR (Response Fig. R23j-3), suggesting that BioCRE-specific predictions are not
only robust but also biologically credible.
Thus, through incorporating external dataset and gold standard chromatin interaction dataset,
we demonstrated that BioCRE exhibits consistent superiority in linkage identification than
Signac and ArchR.
These results have been included in the revised manuscript (Line 162-176; Supplementary
Fig. 4), the detailed method has been provided in Line 982-1038, and we also acknowledged
the significance of systematically benchmark of BioCRE performance and discussed about the
current limitations in Line 623-632, Line 703-705.
Response Figure R23. Benchmark of BioCRE. a. Bar plot showing the number of gene-peak linkages identified by
BioCRE, Signac, and ArchR. b. Histogram showing the median gene-peak distance for linkages identified by BioCRE,
Signac, and ArchR. c. Venn diagram showing the intersection of predicted gene-peak linkages. d. Bar plot highlighting
the ratio of non-overlapping linkage ratios for each tool. e. Gene ontology analyses for BioCRE-specific captured
linkages associated genes. f. UMAP visualization based on the chromatin accessibility of cell type-specific genes
associated peaks. g. Silhouette score evaluating the cell type distribution specificity. h. Line plot depicting the runtime
for each tool with variable proportion of reads. BioCRE was running on a single GPU (A100), while ArchR and Signac
were executed using 20 CPU cores for parallel computing, respectively. i. The effects of sequencing reads down-
sampling on linkage composition consistency for each tool. The constant linkage numbers for each scenario are
highlighted in red. j. The prediction and validation of gene-peak linkages using external multiome dataset and gold
standard promoter-enhancer interaction dataset.
2. Distal vs. Proximal regulatory region comparison: The comparison between "Distal High"
and "Proximal" groups is biased by excluding the "Distal Low" group. A more appropriate
comparison would be between all distal regions and proximal ones, with proper statistical
testing (e.g., p-values) to support conclusions.
Response: Thanks for your constructive suggestion. As recommended, we have directly
compared the JSS score between proximal and distal linked peaks—including both 'distal high'
and 'distal low' groups—thereby providing a more balanced and representative assessment.
Statistical testing (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) confirms that, on average, proximal peaks exhibit
significantly higher JSS scores than distal peaks (Response Fig. R24a), supporting their
stronger association with gene expression variation.
Additionally, we retained the comparison with the "distal high" group as a secondary analysis
to emphasize the particularly strong regulatory potential of this subset, clearly distinguishing it
from the broader distal category. We observed that a considerable number of distal linked
peaks exhibit higher JSS score than those of the proximal peaks (Response Fig. R24b),
highlighting the functional importance of certain distal regulatory elements during gastrulation.
These updated analyses have been incorporated into the Fig. 1f and Supplementary Fig. 5c.
Response Figure R24. Bar plots highlighting the JSS score measuring the consistency between gene
expression and linked peaks. a. The comparison between proximal and distal linked peaks. b. The distal peaks
were subdivided into distal high and distal low group based on the comparison with proximal peaks. Distal peaks were
annotated as peaks located outside TSS ± 2 kb, proximal peaks were annotated as peaks located within TSS ± 2 kb.
Wilcox tests were used to calculate the significances.
3. Insufficient benchmarking for BioCREs and modified Tangram: The manuscript lacks
technical detail and performance benchmarking for both pipelines. More rigorous testing is
needed to demonstrate their robustness and reliability.
Response: Thanks for raising this important issue. We are deeply sorry that the initial
submission lacked sufficient technical details and comprehensive benchmarking.
Regarding BioCRE, we have now conducted an extensive performance evaluation, as detailed
in our response to comment #1 and illustrated in Response Figure R23. This includes
comparisons with established methods—Signac and ArchR—across multiple metrics such as
cell type specificity (Silhouette score), computational efficiency, robustness to various sampling
depth, and accuracy against orthogonal chromatin interaction data (Macro-F1 and TPR scores).
The results consistently demonstrate that BioCRE, built on a bidirectional regression framework,
outperforms the other tools in key aspects relevant to gene-to-peak linkage prediction in
developmental contexts. These analyses have been integrated into the revised manuscript
(Line 162-176; Supplementary Fig. 4) to enhance methodological transparency and rigor.
With respect to the use of Tangram for spatiotemporal mapping, we clarify that our approach
does not involve fundamental modification to the Tangram algorithm itself. Instead, we have
adopted a more refined and biologically informed input strategy, as recommended in the official
Tangram documentation (https://github.com/broadinstitute/Tangram). The refinement strategy
of gene selection for Tangram has been benchmarked in a recent study15. Specifically, rather
than using all genes shared between the Geo-seq and 10x scMultiome datasets, we selected
stage-specific "zipcode" genes — those showing spatially restricted expression patterns during
gastrulation — to improve mapping accuracy. This refinement aligns with best practices and
enhances the biological relevance of the spatial inference (Supplementary Fig. 6c-i). We are
sorry that this aspect was not clearly described in the original submission. We have now
provided the complete list of genes used (Supplementary Table 2) and updated the method
with a detailed and accurate description of using tangram (Line 859-881).
4. Incorporating data from high-resolution platforms such as Visium HD or Stereo-seq
would significantly strengthen the spatial claims.
Response: Thanks for the valuable suggestion. We fully agree that incorporating high-
resolution spatial data, such as Visium HD or Stereo-seq, would strengthen the spatial claims
of the current study.
In this revision, we have incorporated a recently published Stereo-seq dataset (SEU-3D)16
covering the mouse early organogenesis embryos, to which we contributed, for direct
comparison with our ST-MAGIC atlas. As shown, to check the consistency of spatial results
between these two datasets (SEU-3D and ST-MAGIC), we first spatial-temporally aligned the
two datasets, then determined the transcriptional correlation of cell types and spatial
concordance of cell type marker geneset (CTGs) expression, and finally checked the
reproducibility of key spatial findings reported in the current study (Response Fig. R25a).
Generally, spatial transcriptomic data from the E7.5 stage were used, the spatial coordinate
along z-axis (proximal-distal axis) and the cell types annotated in both datasets were aligned
according to their respective sampling strategies (Response Fig. R25b). Pearson correlation
analyses of cell type transcriptome reported that most cell types were well correlated
(Response Fig. R25c). Moreover, the spatial distribution of CTGs were also highly consistent
(Response Fig. R25d). We first present the AUC scores of the top 500 marker gene sets for
each cell types (illustrated for VE, SE, and CE) in SEU-3D, where the spatial distribution of
these scores aligns well with the known anatomical localization of each cell type (first column).
Applying the identical analytical to ST-MAGIC reveals a highly similar spatial pattern (second
column), demonstrating the consistency of marker gene enrichment across reconstruction
methods. To enable a more granular comparison, we then performed a layer-by-layer analysis
relative to Stereo-seq and GEO-seq. For each cell type, we extracted corresponding single-cell
profiles from Stereo-seq and matched them with spot-level single-cell compositions in each
layer of GEO-seq. The similarity between these matched cell populations was assessed using
the marker gene sets. As shown in the results, high similarity is observed at spatially
corresponding locations (third column), while gray regions indicate positions where data were
not jointly present in both datasets. For example, the expression of marker geneset for visceral
endoderm cells were highly enriched in outer layer cells of SEU-3D map and in EA and EP
regions of the ST-MAGIC atlas (Response Fig. R25d). Spatial correlation analysis confirmed
that this enrichment is anatomically coherent, as expression of these markers correlates
obviously only in regions where visceral endoderm is known to reside (Response Fig. R25d).
Then, we checked the spatial distribution of specific cell types and genes between SEU-3D and
ST-MAGIC atlas. As shown in Response Fig. R25e (Fig. 2b in the manuscript), mesenchyme
cells were located at the proximal posterior region and paraxial mesoderm 1 cells were
distributed at the anterior medial mesoderm region according to both ST-MAGIC atlas and
experimental results (Fig. 2b, c). Here, we found that mesenchyme and paraxial mesoderm
cells exhibit similar spatial patterns in SEU-3D atlas. Furthermore, the expression patterns of
canonical markers such as Hand1 (mesenchyme) and Irx5 (paraxial mesoderm) align closely
between the two platforms, further corroborating the accuracy of our ST-MAGIC atlas.
We acknowledge that direct integration is challenged by inherent technical differences: SEU-
3D achieves near single cell bin resolution but with lower transcriptomic depth (~400–600
genes per bin), whereas ST-MAGIC spots capture richer molecular profiles (~3,500–4,500
genes per cell) but at lower spatial resolution (~5 - 10 cells per spot) (Response Fig. R25f).
Due to this disparity in molecular sensitivity, some spatially-restricted, low-abundance
transcripts—such as Wnt3, Nodal and Noto, which are clearly resolved in ST-MAGIC and
supported by prior experimental data—do not exhibit evident expression patterns in SEU-3D
(Response Fig. R25g).
Despite these technical constraints, the overall concordance in cell type localization and gene
expression architecture between SEU-3D and ST-MAGIC strongly supports the robustness of
our spatial reconstructions. We have included the results of cell type spatial allocation in SEU-
3D to demonstrate the credibility of ST-MAGIC in revised Supplementary Fig. 7f and Line
263-266, and also discussed this important issue as
‘Transcriptome coordinate profiling using Stereo-seq17 or MERFISH18, incorporation of
additional data types, such as histone modifications, proteomics, and metabolomics, and
optimizations of bioinformatic toolkits would further enhance the molecular understanding of
early embryogenesis.’
in the revised manuscript (Line 696-700).
Response Figure R25. Incorporation of high resolution spatial transcriptomic data. a. Schematic overview of
the work flow to check the spatial consistency between Stereo-seq dataset (SEU-3D) and ST-MAGIC. b. Temporal,
spatial, cell type alignment between these two datasets. c. Pearson correlation for cell types annotated in both
datasets. d. Spatial concordance of cell type distribution between these two datasets. Three representative cell types
were shown. top: Visceral endoderm; middle: Surface ectoderm; bottom: Caudal epiblast. e. The consistency of
specific spatial claims between SEU-3D and ST-MAGIC atlas. f. Bar plot highlighting the detected nFeature_RNA
per cell in SEU-3D and ST-MAGIC. g. The expression patterns of Wnt3 (left), Nodal (middle), and Noto (right) as
visualized in experimental results, ST-MAGIC, and SEU-3D.

Streamlining these parts would improve accessibility.
Response: Thanks for the comment. In this revision, we have revised the original manuscript

Response: Thanks for the kind reminder. In this revision, we have revised the organization of

Geo-seq is not supported by the figure. This should be clarified or removed.
