## Methods

Ethics statement
Mouse used in this study were housed and bred in the SPF facilities of Guangzhou National Laboratory. All animal experiments were performed in compliance with the guidelines of the Animal Core Facility.

Mouse embryo collection and multi-omic profiling
For embryo sampling, C57BL/6J embryos were harvested from pregnant mice at day 6.5, 6.75, 7.0, 7.25, and 7.5 of gestation (day of vaginal plug detection = Day E0.5). Plugged female mice were picked after mating and marked as embryonic day 0.5 (E0.5). Female mice were sacrificed for embryos collection at specific gestational stages. Embryos were isolated from the uterus and carefully transferred into pre-cool PBS in petri dishes, and surrounding decidua and parietal endoderm tissues were removed using needles under an Olympus stereoscope. Sex of the embryos was not considered in this study.

Careful morphological staging of the acquired embryos was performed before single-cell multi-omic data preparation. The developmental timepoints of embryos were staged by the proximal-distal span of the PS and the anterior-posterior span of the mesoderm layer. To meet the loading requirements for 10x genomics, embryos from the same stage were pooled together and subjected to TrypLE Express enzyme (Gibco, 12604) incubation at 37 °C for 7–10 min. The acquired single-cell suspension was carefully washed and filtered to ensure proper integrity and avoid cell clumping of each single cell. Cell counts were then assessed with a haemocytometer counted under a microscope. Nuclei isolation and multiome library preparation were performed by following the manufacturer’s instructions (https://www.10xgenomics.com/cn/support/single-cell-multiome-atac-plus-gene-expression/documentation).

For the single-cell multi-omic profiling of the Noto KO and Pou6f1 KO embryos, the parents of the heterozygotic mutation were crossed and checked for the vaginal plug. E7.5 embryos were freshly harvested, and a tiny portion of extra embryonic tissues were collected and genotyped. During the genotyping process, the embryos were freshly frozen in liquid nitrogen. Embryos with the same genotypes (WT, Noto KO homozygote, Pou6f1 KO homozygote) were grouped and dissociated into single nuclei. Approximately 15,000 nuclei for each group were collected and loaded for further single-cell multiome library preparation, following the manufacturer’s instructions.

Enhancer activity reporter assay
Generally, the enhancer reporter assay was performed as previously reported4. In brief, DNA fragments for potential regulatory elements were cloned from the C57BL/6J mouse genome and then ligated into the plasmid construct containing the minimal Hsp68 promoter and LacZ. The acquired purified plasmids were then linearized and used for pronuclear injections of PN4 stage zygotes with a FemtoJet Microinjection System (Eppendorf). The injected embryos were cultured to the 2-cell stage in KSOM medium with amino acids at 37 °C under 5% CO2, and then transferred to the oviduct of pseudo-pregnant ICR females and marked as 0.5 dpc. Embryos were collected at the corresponding stage for LacZ staining. LacZ staining was performed using a commercialized β-gal staining kit (Beyotime, RG0039).

RNAscope staining for whole mount or sections of embryo
RNAscope probes including mm-Lefty2-C2 (436291-C2), mm-Hand1-C1 (429651), mm-Irx5-C2 (513871-C2), mm-Isl1-C3 (451931-C3), mm-Sox2-C1 (401041-C1), mm-Otx2-C3 (444381-C3), mm-T-C3 (423511-C3), mm-Eomes-C2 (429641-C2), mm-Foxa2-C4 (409111-C4), mm-Shh-C2 (314361-C2), mm-Noto-C3 (1253281-C3), mm-Foxj1-C3 (317091-C3), mm-Dynlrb2-C3 (1243011-C3), mm-Col2a1-C4 (407221-C4), mm-Rsph9-C2 (430201-C2), and mm-Pou6f1-C1 (801931-C1) were bought from the Advanced Cell Diagnostics.

For whole mount RNAscope staining, embryos were fixed in 4% PFA overnight. After serial dehydration and rehydration of embryos using gradient methanol-PBS solution, embryos were subject to the RNAscope protocol following the manufacturer’s instruction (https://acdbio.com/sites/default/files/MK%2050016%20Zebrafish_WISH_Tech%20Note_12042017.pdf). Images of stained embryos were acquired using the LiTone XL system (Light Innovation Technology Limited).

For RNAscope staining with embryo sections, dissected embryos were first fixed in 4% PFA, then dehydrated in 20% Sucrose-PBS and 30% Surcrose-PBS solution, respectively. The dehydrated embryos were embedded in OCT matrix and then cryo-sectioned using Leica CM1950. RNAscope workflow was performed by following the manufacturer’s instructions (https://acdbio.com/ebook/introduction/materialsmethod). Images were acquired by using the Carl Zeiss LSM980 system.

Wholemount in situ hybridization
Wholemount in situ hybridization of RNA transcripts was performed by following the published protocol61. Briefly, DNA fragments encoding the probes of Lety2 were firstly PCR amplified by using the oligos in Supplementary Data 7 using a mouse embryo cDNA library. Embryos at relevant stages were collected in DMEM media and then fixed in 4% PFA at 4 °C overnight. Fixed embryos were then washed in PBS solution at room temperature to remove residual PFA, followed by serial dehydration and rehydration in PBS, 25% Methanol/PBS, 50% Methanol/PBS, 75% Methanol/PBS, and 100% Methanol. Afterward, the embryos were treated with 10 μg/mL proteinase K and incubated with DIG-labeled RNA probes at 70 °C overnight. To remove the remaining RNA probes, embryos were washed in TBST buffer with frequent buffer changing for at least 2–4 h. Then the embryos were incubated with anti-DIG-AP antibody at 4 °C overnight. The embryos were subjected to sufficient TBST wash before final staining with NBT and BCIP solution. The final images of stained embryos were collected using an Olympus SZX16 microscope.

The generation of genome edited mouse embryonic stem cell or mouse model
In this study, we have prepared the genome-edited mouse embryonic stem cell lines with Mesp1 Neo_ME element, Mesp1 EME element, and Lefty2 Neo_LRE element knockout, respectively. The CRISPR-Cas9 system was used to generate the genome-edited mouse embryonic stem cell lines. Guided RNAs were designed by using the online tool Chop-chop (http://chopchop.cbu.uib.no/). The synthesized sgRNA DNA fragments were then ligated into the px330 plasmid with a Cas9 protein expression cassette. The acquired purified plasmids were then transfected into the WT cells using Lipofectamine 3000. The genome-edited clones were then selected and genotyped as previously reported62. The potential off-target editing sites were tested based on the website’s indication.

To determine the roles of Pou6f1, we also generated a mouse model with Pou6f1 deletion. The specific sequences for sgRNA pairs were included in Supplementary Data 7. DNA fragments for the sgRNA and T7-Cas9 were transcribed and purified in vitro using MMESSAGE MMACHINE T7 Ultra Kit (Invitrogen, AM1345) and MEGAclear kit (Invitrogen, AM1908). To prepare a sufficient number of fertilized zygotes, C57BL/6J female mice (4 weeks old) were superovulated and mated with the male C57BL/6 mice. Twenty-four hours later, fertilized embryos were collected from the oviducts. RNA for Cas9 protein (100 ng/µl) and corresponding sgRNA (100 ng/µl) were mixed in HEPES-CZB medium containing 5 μg/ml cytochalasin B (CB) and injected into the cytoplasm of fertilized eggs using a FemtoJet microinjector (Eppendorf) with constant flow settings. The injected embryos were cultured in KSOM with amino acids at 37 °C under 5% CO2 in the air to reach the 2-cell stage after 24 h in vitro. Two-cell embryos were transferred into pseudo-pregnant ICR female mice. The acquired mouse individuals were then subjected to genotyping for successful Pou6f1 deletion. Mice with Pou6f1 deletion were retained and recorded as F0. To prepare the stable Pou6f1 deletion mouse line, F0 mice were crossed, and the acquired F1 mice were checked. Pou6f1 KO heterozygotes F1 mice were maintained, and the population was expanded for the following experiments.

The Noto KO mouse line was purchased from GemPharmatech (Strain ID: T017401).

Scanning electron microscopy
Embryo samples were freshly collected and fixed in 2.5% glutaraldehyde overnight at 4 °C. Subsequently, the samples were thoroughly washed with PBS four times at 10-minute intervals to ensure the complete removal of the fixative. Fixed embryos were treated with osmium tetroxide for 1 h to enhance the contrast and stability of cellular structures under the electron beam. The samples were then washed with ddH2O five times at 10 min intervals to remove any residual osmium tetroxide. Dehydrate the embryos in an ethanol series for 5–10 min each: 50%, 70%, 85%, and three times in 100%. Transferred the embryos in ethanol to baskets for critical point drying (CPD) in a critical point dryer machine (Quorum K850 critical point dryer). After that, the samples were mounted on sample stubs and sputter-coated with gold using a Quorum Q150RS sputter coater. Finally, the samples were imaged using the Zeiss GeminiSEM 300 scanning electron microscope.

The ST-MAGIC atlas
Pre-processing of Geo-seq and 10x scMultiome: The Geo-seq data utilized in this study were obtained from our previously published datasets, specifically including E6.5, E7.0, and E7.5 from GSE120963, and E6.75, E7.25, and E7.5 (left-right resolved) from GSE171588. The five stages of 10x scMultiome data were newly generated in this study. For the Geo-seq data, the quantification of the FASTQ files was performed using RSEM (v1.3.3), leveraging annotations from the Cell Ranger GTF file. The normalized TPM values were processed using the ‘NormalizeData’ function in the Seurat (v4.1.1) package and were then used for further analytical procedures. For the scMultiome data, the normalized snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq data were processed using Seurat and Signac (v1.6.0) and were subsequently employed for further analytical procedures.

Alignment of 10x scMultiome to Geo-seq: The alignment of snRNA-seq data to Geo-spatial spots was achieved using Tangram (v 1.0.4), with the precise spatial location of each cell determined from the mapping matrix with the highest probability. The gene expression of each reconstructed spot was obtained by averaging the gene expression levels of the cells mapped to the indicated spot, and the gene expression percentage of a spot represents the proportion of cells within the indicated spot that express the gene (gene reads > 0). For snATAC-seq data mapping, the spatial location of each cell from snRNA-seq is shared. The peak accessibility of each reconstructed spot was obtained by averaging the peak accessibility level of the cells mapped to the indicated spot, and the peak accessibility percentage of a spot represents the ratio of cells within the indicated spot with an open peak (peak reads > 0). The cell type distribution was obtained using the tg.project_cell_annotations function within the Tangram toolkit, and the cell type percentage of a spot represents the ratio of cells of that type within the spot.

In the application of Tangram, the training genes are specified as the zipcode genes relevant to each stage, and the mapping strategy is customized for individual cells. For the E6.5 and E6.75 embryos, the top 100 cell-type marker genes identified by the COSG (v 0.9.0) package63 were designated as zipcode genes. For the E7.0, E7.25, and E7.5 embryos, the PC loading genes calculated by the Seurat package (E7.0, top 500 highest and 500 lowest genes of PC1-10; E7.25, top 50 highest and 50 lowest genes of PC1-10; E7.5, top 500 highest and 500 lowest genes of PC1-5) were designated as zipcode genes. The zipcode list has been provided in Supplementary Data 2.

Since Geo-seq primarily captures the proximal to distal embryonic regions of the gastrula, cell types from the scMultiome data that is not present within these zones were excluded from the analysis. Specifically, the following cell types were filtered out: ExE endoderm, ExE ectoderm, Haematoendothelial progenitors, Blood progenitors 1, and Blood progenitors 2.

Smooth of corn plot: The smoothing of mapped features in ST-MAGIC is achieved through Gaussian weighting of neighboring spots, including the mapped feature smooth denoted as F and the percent smooth denoted as P, defined as:
F_smooth = Σ n j=1 w i,j (θ) × F j, w i,j (θ) = e - ||Fi - Fj||2 / 2θ2
P_smooth = Σ n j=1 w i,j (θ) × P j, w i,j (θ) = e - ||Pi - Pj||2 / 2θ2

For the selection of neighboring spots, ST-MAGIC provides three types of input: column neighboring spots along the proximal-distal axis by default, row neighboring spots along the anterior-posterior axis, and customized neighboring spots. The query is designed to recognize user-defined consistent patterns, whether they are genes, peaks, or cell types. The spatial pattern of interest was defined in binary, with the value of the corresponding spot set to 1 and the value of all other spots set to 0. Similar omics data matching this binary pattern were selected using cosine similarity, as implemented in the COSG package. For example, ST-MAGIC detects the specified peaks in customized RPM and LPM regions (distal peaks in the left and right proximal mesoderm regions shown in Fig. 2g, h). This process will facilitate the identification of spatiotemporally regulated patterns in individual cells.

The ST-MAGIC(+) atlas
Calculation of enrichment score: Building on the single gene or peak analysis capabilities of ST-MAGIC, ST-MAGIC (+) extends these features by enabling the spatial monitoring of gene sets and peak sets from SCEINIC+ or public resources through enrichment analysis by the AUCell (v1.18.1) package. The enrichment of gene sets and peak sets of each spot was obtained by averaging the AUC score of the cells mapped to that spot, and the enrichment percentage of a spot represents the average ratio of expressed genes or accessible peaks within that spot.

Spatial signaling responsiveness pattern: The binding of signaling molecules to multiple genomic regions highlights the complexity and interconnectedness of gene regulatory networks. It highlights how single factors can coordinate with diverse downstream targets to orchestrate cellular responses and developmental programs. ST-MAGIC(+) enables the depiction of the spatial activities of signaling responsiveness, such as WNT and Nodal (Fig. 4), using data from public ChIP-seq datasets. Before calculating the AUC score, the peaks from public datasets must first be aligned to those identified in our own dataset using the GenomicRanges (v1.48.0) package to ensure a consistent genomic context for comparative analysis.

BioCRE model
The construction of BioCRE: Unlike published tools that detect CREs using only a single peak or a single gene, BioCRE employs a systematic approach to calculate these linkages. BioCRE harnesses a bi-orientation regression model leveraging multi-omics data decoding GRN at the chromosome level to identify potential CREs.

To formulate the linear optimization procedure using paired snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq data, let Gθ ∈ Rg×n denotes snRNA-seq data profiling g genes across n cells on a given chromosome θ, let Pθ ∈ Rp×n denotes snATAC-seq data with p peaks for the same set of n cells on the chromosome θ. We assumed the linkage matrix Lθ ∈ Rg×p is the cis-regulation between genes and peaks on chromosome θ. Our goal is to learn the linkage matrix L that captures cis-regulation under two conditions: (1) the predicted snRNA-seq matrix G^θ, generated using the linkage matrix Lθ and snATAC-seq matrix Pθ, should be similar to the real snRNA matrix Gθ; (2) the predicted snATAC-seq matrix P^θ, generated using the linkage matrix Lθ and snRNA matrix Gθ, should be similar to the real snATAC-seq matrix Pθ. We minimize the following cost function as:
arg min Lθ ∈ {chr1, chr2, ..., chrY} (E ||Gθ - G^θ||2 + E ||Pθ - P^θ||2 + λθ × REG loss)

The cost function consists of three parts:
1) The expected loss between the real snRNA-seq matrix Gθ and the predicted snRNA-seq matrix G^θ:
E ||Gθ - G^θ||2 = Σg i=1 Σn k=1 (Gθ i,k - G^θ i,k)2 = Σg i=1 Σn k=1 (Gθ i,k - Σp j=1 Lθ i,j × Pθ j,k)2
Where Gθ i,k is the expression level of gene i in cell k on chromosome θ, Pθ j,k is the chromatin accessibility of peak j in cell k on chromosome θ, the Lθ i,j is the strength of linkage between gene i and peak j on chromosome θ.
2) The expected loss between the real snATAC-seq matrix Pθ and the predicted snATAC-seq matrix P^θ:
E ||Pθ - P^θ||2 = Σp j=1 Σn k=1 (Pθ j,k - P^θ j,k)2 = Σp j=1 Σn k=1 (Pθ j,k - Σg i=1 Lθ i,j × Gθ i,k)2
3) The L2 regularization loss of the linkage matrix Lθ with hyperparameter λθ:
REG loss = ||Lθ||2 = sqrt(Σg i=1 Σp j=1 (Lθ i,j)2)

Under this model, we systematically considered all combinations of genes and peaks within the same chromosome, effectively simulating the complexity of GRN.

To mitigate the risk of gradient vanishing in a model with a large number of parameters, ‘He’ initialization was employed for the weight matrices:
W ∼ N(0, 2/p)
Where p is the number of peaks. The L-BFGS algorithm is employed to achieve the minimization of the cost function, the training process is configured for 500 epochs with a learning rate of 0.5.

After the optimization of L, the extraction of significant linkages is required. Firstly, we computed bi-orientation p-values, which involved assessing the significance of a given CRE in relation to all CREs linked to the same gene by z-score, followed by evaluating its significance among all CREs associated with the same peak, the p-values were adjusted using the Bonferroni correction method applied separately to each set of comparisons. Then, the two p-values are combined into a single value through Pearson’s method in the ‘SciPy’ package:
-2 Σn i=1 log(1 - pi)
Finally, the CREs are constrained to those within a 1 megabase range, and only those with a combined p-value less than 10-7 are reserved.

Benchmark analysis of BioCRE
Performance on gastrula multi-omic dataset: In the absence of a genome-wide gold standard for gene-to-peak linkages in the mouse gastrula, we used the Jensen-Shannon Similarity score, which is calculated based on the Jensen-Shannon Divergence index, to evaluate the concordance between genes and peaks in linkage for BioCRE, compared to linkages established using default parameters in ArchR and Signac. The JSS score of each linkage was calculated using the normalized gene expression Gi from snRNA data and the peak accessibility Pj from snATAC data across n cells.
JSS = 1 - E(G, P) = 1 - (sqrt(E(G) + E(P)) - sqrt(E(G + P))) / 2
E(P) = - Σn k=1 pk × log(pk)

The JSS score was also used to evaluate the robustness of the ST-MAGIC atlas, which maps snRNA-seq data to Geo-seq data. Specifically, it assessed the concordance between the reconstructed gene expression in spot from the snRNA-seq and the raw gene expression in spot from the Geo-seq data.

In addition, we computed the silhouette score to evaluate the effectiveness of cell type-specific gene-linked peaks in clustering cells in UMAP visualizations. Using pre-annotated cell types as clustering labels, the silhouette score was calculated based on the 2nd to 10th latent semantic indexing components via the ‘cluster’ package. A higher silhouette score indicates that cells of the same type are more closely grouped.

To systematically evaluate the stability and robustness of BioCRE in predicting CREs across varying sequencing depths, comprehensive down-sampling experiments were conducted. Initially, paired single-cell transcriptomic (snRNA-seq) and single-cell chromatin accessibility (snATAC-seq) datasets were jointly down-sampled to 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100% of their original sequencing depth. This allowed for an assessment of prediction consistency across methods under increasingly sparse data conditions. Subsequently, two complementary experimental paradigms were implemented: first, snATAC-seq data were maintained at full depth while the sequencing depth of snRNA-seq was progressively reduced; second, snRNA-seq data were preserved in their entirety while the depth of snATAC-seq data was incrementally decreased. In all experimental conditions, the stability of predicted regulatory linkages was quantitatively evaluated based on the proportion of shared linkages identified across different sequencing depths.

Performance on public multi-omic datasets with corresponding promoter capture Hi-C data: To systematically compare the predictive performance of BioCRE, we conducted additional evaluations using publicly available data. We analyzed published multi-omics datasets (PBMC: https://www.10xgenomics.com/cn/datasets/pbmc-from-a-healthy-donor-granulocytes-removed-through-cell-sorting-10-k-1-standard-1-0-0 and GM12878: GSE166797), with corresponding promoter capture Hi-C data (PBMC: EGAS00001001911 and GM12878: https://zenodo.org/records/3255048) as reference datasets for validating predicted linkages.

Standardized genomic scope of predicted linkages across all three tools were restricted to ±500kb upstream and downstream of the gene body. Notably, although the total numbers of predicted linkages are theoretically consistent across methods, minor discrepancies may arise due to each tool’s internal preprocessing steps—such as gene and peak filtering—which may exclude certain elements prior to linkage inference. The filtered geneset and peakset shared by all three tools were used for further linkage prediction.

For comparison between the public multi-omic datasets and the reference dataset, any predicted linkages overlapping the reference set was considered as positives, while non-overlapping linkages were treated as negatives. Due to the distinct features for different data modules between the predicted linkages and the reference dataset (PCHiC), the overlap is inherently limited, leading to a sparse set of positive linkages. Here, to ensure balanced and robust evaluation, we randomly sampled negative linkages ten times at each positive-to-negative ratio. Specifically, for the PBMC dataset, we evaluated the AUPRC through ‘sklearn.metrics’ package under varying positive-to-negative ratios: 1:1, 1:2, 1:3, 1:4, and 1:5. For GM12878, we used ratios of 1:1 and 1:2, as the larger number of positive linkages—relative to PBMC—split the accessibility of AUPRC. Besides, we used the p-value for BioCRE, the p-value for Signac, and the FDR for ArchR.

Multi-omics data pre-processing
Raw FASTQ files of snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq were processed by Cell Ranger ARC (v2.0.1) with default mapping parameters. Reads were mapped to the mouse reference genome (mm10) and quantified with gene annotation (GRCm38.98). The quality control of snRNA-seq and snATAC-seq data was performed separately, retaining only high-quality cells that passed both criteria for subsequent analyses. For snRNA-seq data, the following quality control criteria were applied: (1) cells that had fewer than 1000 expressed genes, or over 10% of UMIs derived from mitochondrial genome were removed; (2) cells identified as doublet (DoubletFinder, v2.0.3) were removed; (3) clusters generated by Seurat using default parameters were removed if AY036118 and Gm42418 genes were highly expressed. For snATAC-seq data, cells were required to have a minimum of 3000 fragments, a minimum fraction of fragments in peaks of 0.15, a minimum of TSS enrichment of 9, a maximum of blacklist ratio of 0.05 and a maximum of nucleosomal signal strength of 4.

snRNA-seq processing
After converting the filtered snRNA-seq count matrix to a Seurat object, the standard procedures were performed using the Seurat package. For each stage (E6.5, E6.75, E7.0, E7.25, and E7.5), the following analysis steps were applied: (1) the count matrix was log-normalized for each cell with a scaling factor of 10,000; (2) 2000 variable genes were selected by ‘vst’ method; (3) the ‘nFeature_RNA’ was regressed out during the scaling process. For the combined dataset, the ‘stage’, ‘nFeature_RNA’, and ‘percent.mt’ were regressed out; (4) The scaled variable genes were projected into a low-dimensional space using principal component analysis; (5) The shared nearest neighbor (SNN) graph was built based on the distance of PC space (nPCs=50); (6) The Louvain algorithm was used to identify clusters based on SNN graph (resolution=1); (7) The UMAP embedding was calculated using ‘uwot’ with the top 10 PCs.

snATAC-seq processing
As the precise boundaries of peaks differed across embryonic stages, a common set of peaks (20 bp < length of peak < 10,000 bp) across all stages was generated using the ‘reduce’ function in GenomicRanges (v1.48.0) package. The fragment file was then remapped to these common peaks to get the chromatin accessibility matrix. Then, the remapped chromatin accessibility matrix and correspondent fragment file were processed using the Signac package. The matrix was normalized by Term Frequency Inverse Document Frequency, and all peaks were used for dimension reduction using Singular Value Decomposition. The UMAP embedding was computed utilizing dimensions from 2 to 10, with min.dist set to 0.2.

Clustering and cell type annotation
The annotation of multi-omics is based on snRNA-seq data, while snATAC-seq annotation is facilitated via the consistent cellular barcodes between the transcriptome and chromatin accessibility data, ensuring harmonized identification across datasets. Given that cell type diversification during gastrulation, the cell types of snRNA-seq data were annotated in a stage-by-stage manner. Initially, the snRNA-seq data is clustered through the standard Seurat pipeline (vars.to.regress=‘nFeature_RNA’, k.param=20, dims=1:10, resolution=1) with a preliminary annotation to the three primary groups: Embryonic, ExE endoderm, and ExE ectoderm, then cells within the Embryonic group were subjected to an iterative clustering process to achieve more finely detailed cell types. The iterative clustering also employs the Seurat pipeline (vars.to.regress=c(‘nFeature_RNA’, ‘percent.mt’), k.param=30, dims=1:30, resolution=0.9, these parameters remain constant throughout the iterative process) to conduct a clustering process independently on each cluster, with the stipulation that clusters cannot be further subdivided or any cluster containing fewer than 50 cells will not be subjected to additional clustering. Following several iterations, the definitive clusters are established. The integration of cluster-specific genes (defined by the COSG algorithm63) and marker genes from the published gastrulation transcriptome atlas3,6 were mainly used to annotate the clusters. Ambiguous clusters were clarified by correlating them with the closest matching cell type found in existing public datasets (GSE87038). The integration of the public dataset with our snRNA-seq data is facilitated through the use of Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) within the Seurat package. The Pearson correlation between the pseudo-bulk transcriptomic profiles of our iterative clusters and those of cell types in the public dataset is employed to refine annotations.

The similarity between snRNA-seq data and published datasets
To verify the reliability of the annotation, we compared it with the public dataset (GSE87038) at three levels: the proportion of cell types, the correlation of marker genes, and the correlation of the whole transcriptome. First, the shared stages and corresponding cell type data were extracted from the public dataset. Then, the CCA method in Seurat was used to integrate these two datasets. The proportion of each cell type and the expression of marker genes (Sox2, Mesp1, Sox17, and Hnf4a) were statistically compared between the two datasets, along with the pseudo-bulk expression of 2000 high-variance genes across cell types.

Cellular trajectory analysis with TOME
The cellular trajectory spanning from E3.5 to E7.5 was reconstructed based on scRNA/snRNA-seq data using the TOME. The processed dataset covering the developmental stages from E3.5 to E6.25 was made available by the TOME. For the subsequent stages from E6.5 to E7.5, we employed our snRNA-seq data. The identification of the nearest ancestral node for each subsequent stage node is repeated for 500 times based on 50 nearest neighbors. Only those edges with a probability greater than 0.2 will be preserved. Given that the annotated cell types do not align perfectly with those in the pre-stage dataset, we have designated “Embryonic visceral endoderm” as “visceral endoderm,” and “Extraembryonic visceral endoderm” as “ExE endoderm” within our dataset for consistency.

WNN embedding for embryonic cells
The RNA and ATAC modality from embryonic cells, mapping to Geo-seq data, across five development stages, were integrated to construct a weighted nearest neighbor graph by the ‘FindMultiModalNeighbors’ method in the Seurat package. In the snRNA-seq data process, the ‘stage’, ‘nFeature_RNA’, and ‘percent.mt’ were regressed out during normalizing. In snATAC-seq data process, the ‘min.cutoff’ was set to ‘q0’ in finding top features.

Inference of the TF regulatory network with SCENIC+
The pre-processed multi-omic RNA and ATAC matrices, encompassing the full dataset and axial mesendoderm lineages, are utilized as inputs for SCENIC+ (v 0.1.dev452), facilitating the construction of the TF regulatory network. SCENIC+ was executed with the majority of its settings at their default values, with adjustments made only to parameters specific to the dataset. For the full dataset, the peak matrix is regenerated utilizing stage-specific cell type pseudobulk data through MACS2 (v2.2.7.1). During the cisTopic (v1.0.2) module, an optimized set of 16 topics is selected for further analysis. Peaks within a 2kb~500kb range upstream or downstream of genes are incorporated into the SCENIC+ modeling process. eRegulons featuring positive region-to-gene associations, along with a correlation exceeding 0.15 between the TF cistrome and region-based activity, were retained, resulting in a set of 302 high-quality eRegulons. For axial mesendoderm lineages, stage-specific peaks for each cell type are also generated. In cisTopic, the optimized number of topics is set at 16. The range for peaks is consistent with that of the full datasets. eRegulons are retained based on a correlation threshold of 0.15 between the TF cistrome and region-based activity, yielding a total of 118 high-quality eRegulons.

Differential ChIP-seq peaks of the NODAL and WNT signaling
For each ChIP-seq dataset, raw sequencing data was downloaded from the relative resource (NODAL signaling: GSE70486; WNT signaling: GSE43565, GSE162774) and then mapped to the mouse genome (mm10). Peak calling was performed against the corresponding input sample using MACS with the parameters “--shiftsize=100 --nomodel --keep-dup=all”. Subsequently, we merged all resulting peaks of samples into a consensus list of genomic regions and counted the reads within those regions using MAnorm2_utils (v1.0.0) with the parameters “--min-peak-gap=150 --typical-bin-size=2000 --shiftsize=100 --filter=blacklist”. The blacklist regions of mm10 were obtained from Amemiya et al.64. Then, MAnorm2 (v 1.2.2) were used to perform differential peak analysis between samples with default parameters (refer to https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/MAnorm2/vignettes/MAnorm2_vignette.html). The differential peaks were identified using the cutoffs adjusted p-value < 0.01 and fold change > 2.

Axial mesendoderm lineage cells
The selection of axial mesendoderm lineage cells was guided by trajectory analysis depicted in Fig. 1c. This lineage originates from the primitive streak cells at E6.5, and subsequently progresses through the Anterior primitive streak at E6.75 and E7.0. It then developed into Node precursors and Anterior mesendoderm precursors at E7.25. The lineage culminates at E7.5 with Node and Anterior mesendoderm. To ensure more reliable lineage-related cells, we retain only those cells from ancestral stages that are found among the nearest neighbors as calculated by TOME, except for cells in the E6.5 Primitive streak.

Driver genes of axial mesendoderm lineage with CellRank
The sorted BAM files derived from CellRanger were processed using Velocyto (v0.17.17) to compute RNA velocities for individual cells. The mask GTF file was obtained from the UCSC database, and the genome annotation file originates from CellRanger. This procedure enables detailed analysis of transcriptional dynamics at the single-cell level by leveraging the spliced and unspliced transcript information contained within the BAM files. The velocity matrix specific to the axial mesendoderm lineage cells has been extracted from the loom file utilizing the SeuratWrappers (v 0.3.0) R package. Subsequently, the velocity matrix was employed for velocity estimation through the application of the ‘dynamical’ model in scVelo (v0.2.5). The cell-cell transition matrix was calculated employing the ‘cellrank.tl.transition_matrix’ function in CellRank (v 1.5.1). Terminal states were set as Node and Anterior mesendoderm manually. Following this, the GPCCA estimator was utilized to compute both the fate probabilities and driver genes. The top 1000 smoothed driver genes, which exhibited the highest correlation with pseudotime, were selected as the key drivers. The driver genes identified in the BioCRE linkage analysis of the axial mesendoderm lineage and their linked peaks were selected to plot the heatmap. The pseudotime for the lineage was computed utilizing the ‘scanpy.tl.dpt’ function (scanpy, v 1.9.1), incorporating the eRegulon RNA and ATAC AUC matrices obtained from the SCENIC+.

KO-omics data processing
The preprocessing for KO-omics data (WT, Noto KO, Pou6f1 KO embryos at the E7.5 stage) is consistent with those previously mentioned. The annotation method for WT snRNA-seq data remains consistent with the previous approach, whereas for Noto KO and Pou6f1 KO samples, snRNA-seq annotation is performed using the ‘MapQuery’ in Seurat, with annotated WT snRNA-seq data serving as a reference. The annotation for snATAC-seq data was aligned with that of snRNA-seq by leveraging shared cell barcodes.

Web server implementation
The 10x scMultiome data and reconstructed Geo-seq data are available through the ST-MAGIC web server, which was implemented using Shinyapps from R. This web service provides three main functionalities: (1) Transcriptomics in snRNA-seq data, which illustrates gene expression on UMAP and cell type grouping; (2) Epigenomics in snATAC-seq data, which shows peak accessibility, linkage, and motif information; (3) Spatial omics of multiome data, which includes gene, peak, cell type, gene set, and peak set enrichment visualized on a corn plot. ST-MAGIC enables users to explore spatial and temporal patterns in a user-friendly manner. For transcriptomics, profiled genes can be searched for their expression patterns over space and time. For epigenomics, profiled peaks and motifs can be used to investigate spatial and temporal accessibility patterns. In addition, ST-MAGIC provides a selection list of gene sets or peak sets from SCENIC+ to TF enrichment analysis.

In “Spatiotemporal Regulatory Logics of Mouse Gastrulation”, Yang et al describe two resources, ST-MAGIC and ST-MAGIC+, that project new single cell multimodal transcriptome and ATAC-seq data collected for 4 timepoints between E6.5-E7.5 during mouse gastrulation onto the published Geo-seq spatial profiling atlas. To identify gene regulatory networks, the authors introduce a new software package, BioCRE, to analyze multimodal transcriptome information with ATAC-seq data to link genes with accessibility peaks. The authors describe several vignettes including dissection of the GRNs and enhancers that guide mesendoderm development to showcase how these resources can be used. Through those vignettes, they identify novel enhancer elements and transcription factors that may affect differentiation.

The manuscript is a tour-de-force work integrating many published data sets and tools. Indeed, most figures both in the main text and supplementary had a very large number of panels. The manuscript was reasonably well written so that I could follow the logic through analysis of this complex data set and I commend the authors for providing many data panels. The schematics as the first panel for several figures was helpful. Moreover, I appreciated the generation of new data to follow up new hypotheses (Pou6f1 KO and Noto KO multi-seq data) and the RNA-scope experiments for validation.

Nonetheless, it was difficult to assess many of the claims due to a lack of quantification, statistical tests, and useful visualizations. While the development of new analysis platforms like BioCRE is useful, BioCRE was not adequately benchmarked against other methods and so it is difficult to evaluate its contribution to this manuscript.

### Reviewer 2

In this manuscript, Yang and colleagues present a spatiotemporal dataset capturing mouse gastrulation, generated using 10x Genomics Multiome data. The study involves a significant amount of data integration and projection, incorporating external datasets such as Geo-seq and ChIP-seq. To enable gene regulatory network (GRN) analysis, the authors developed a new computational tool called BioCREs, which they claim performs better than existing pipelines. They also adapted the Tangram algorithm—originally designed for high-resolution spatial transcriptomics—for use with their data to align it with Geo-seq references. Through this combined approach, they aim to map spatial and temporal regulatory changes during gastrulation.

The scope of this work is impressive, and the integration of multiple data types is interesting. The authors also acknowledge the limitations of current spatial resolution and mismatched cell type references, which are important caveats. I appreciate the validation experiments included, which lend support to some of their conclusions. That said, I do have several concerns, especially regarding the BioCREs pipeline and the modified Tangram tool.

Major Concerns:
1. The claim that BioCREs outperforms Signac and ArchR is based on a single performance index. This is insufficient to justify the claim. Benchmarking against established regulatory element datasets (e.g., ENCODE) is necessary to validate accuracy and specificity.
2. Distal vs. Proximal regulatory region comparison: The comparison between "Distal High" and "Proximal" groups is biased by excluding the "Distal Low" group. A more appropriate comparison would be between all distal regions and proximal ones, with proper statistical testing (e.g., p-values) to support conclusions.
3. Insufficient benchmarking for BioCREs and modified Tangram: The manuscript lacks technical detail and performance benchmarking for both pipelines. More rigorous testing is needed to demonstrate their robustness and reliability.
4. Incorporating data from high-resolution platforms such as Visium HD or Stereo-seq would significantly strengthen the spatial claims. Even one matching experiment would add credibility.

Minor Comments:
• The manuscript is dense, especially in later sections discussing biological processes. Streamlining these parts would improve accessibility.
• Some extended data figures are poorly organized and should be revised for clarity.
• Clarity in Extended Data Fig. 2a: The plot is overcrowded due to overlapping cells, making it difficult to interpret. A side-by-side comparison with reference data in separate panels would improve readability.
• Missing data in Extended Fig. 4: The claim that ST-MAGIC has higher JSD values than Geo-seq is not supported by the figure. This should be clarified or removed.

abundance genes.

index, P-value) and versatile plots (histogram, scatter plot, density plot) to quantitatively
evaluate the global similarities between ST-MAGIC and Geo-seq atlas, and

and eRegulons. Overall, the original spatial claims have been substantially strengthened.
4. We conducted additional gastruloid differentiation experiments to determine the roles of

significances for Noto mutant and Pou6f1 mutant embryos. Consequently, we
demonstrated the roles of Neo_LRE in regulating Lefty2 expression, and confirmed the
axis turning defects of Noto mutant and Pou6f1 mutant embryos.

Lines 154-165: There is not enough analysis benchmarking BioCRE against Signac and ArchR.
What other metrics can be used to measure the consistency of gene expression and peaks?
What are the set characteristics between the linkage predictions of the three tools (does
BioCRE identify a super set of linkage? Are many predictions non-overlapping?). What are the
run-time characteristics for BioCRE compared to the other tools? How does sampling affect
BioCRE performance? Example: downsample the RNA-seq and ATAC-seq together, down-
sample one while holding the other constant, etc. How does the median gene-to-peak distance
compare between methods?
Response: Thanks for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree that a more comprehensive
benchmarking strategy is essential to substantiate our claim that BioCRE outperforms existing
tools.
In this revision, to benchmark the performance of BioCRE, we have conducted a series of
systematic evaluations to rigorously compare the performance of BioCRE against the state-of-
the-art methods: Signac and ArchR.
1. The characteristics of predicted gene-to-peak linkages:
Using our multi-omic dataset from the mouse gastrula, we evaluated the number, biological
relevance, and cell type specificity of predicted gene-to-peak linkages. As shown, BioCRE
identified 44,644 gene-to-peak linkages, with a median gene-to-peak distance of 127,175 bp
(Response Fig. R3a, b). Comparative analyses revealed that 28,472 linkages (64%) were
specifically identified in BioCRE (Response Fig. R3c, d). Gene ontology analyses of genes
associated with these BioCRE-specific linkages (28,472 linkages) revealed significant
enrichment in embryo development, including heart development, liver development, and
nervous system development (Response Fig. R3e). This result suggests that these BioCRE-
specific linkages could be responsible for the regulation of embryo development related genes.
To assess the cell type specificity of predicted linkages, we analyzed the accessibility of peaks
linked to cell type-specific genes identified by each tool (Response Fig. R3f, g). Using UMAP
visualization and quantifying clustering coherence with the Silhouette score, we found that
linkages predicted by BioCRE gets a higher score compared to those from Signac and ArchR,
indicating a more effective capability for BioCRE to capture cell type-specific linkages
(Response Fig. R3f, g).
Together, these results demonstrate that BioCRE could be adept at identify cell type-specific
linkages, which are likely to play key roles in orchestrating embryo development.
2. The computational efficiency and robustness for predicting linkages:
We assessed the computational efficiency and robustness of different methods under varying
sampling conditions. Overall, we found that the built-in deep-learning bi-orientation regression
model for BioCRE does not incur excessive run-time costs, showing comparable performance
to ArchR (Response Fig. R3h). To evaluate the robustness of linkage identification, we
checked the consistency of predicted linkages across three distinct down-sampling scenarios:
 In the first scenario, where both RNA and peak reads were down-sampled concurrently,
BioCRE demonstrated the highest recovery rate of linkage identification (Response Fig.
R3i). To specify, 40.9% linkages (31,911 out of 78,109) are constantly identified in BioCRE,
while only 8.2% linkages (3,677 out of 44,705) for Signac and 5.7% linkages (4,479 out of
79,067) for ArchR show consistent results among variable sample sizes (Response Fig.
R3i-1).
 In the second scenario, where only RNA reads were down-sampled while peak reads
remain unchanged, we found that 44.6% linkages (21,406 out of 48,043) are consistently
captured for BioCRE (Response Fig. R3i-2). In the meantime, 42.9% linkages (18,335
out of 42,937) for Signac and 61.9% linkages (38,510 out of 62,226) for ArchR are stably
identified (Response Fig. R3i-2).
 In the last scenario, we specifically down-sampled peak reads and then performed linkage
identification (Response Fig. R3i-3). Consequently, we found that 52.1% linkages
(49,476/95,042) for BioCRE are captured across all down-sampling groups (Response
Fig. R3i-3). In contrast, only 24.1% linkages (9,122/37,894) for Signac and 46.2% linkages
(28,388/61,422) for ArchR show the same pattern (Response Fig. R3i-3).
Collectively, these analyses demonstrate that BioCRE achieves a favorable balance between
computational efficiency and robustness, exhibiting consistency and high reproducibility in
linkage prediction across diverse and reduced sequencing depths—particularly under
conditions of limited chromatin accessibility data (Scenario 1 and 3)—highlighting its reliability
in practical, resource-variable settings.
3. The reliability and accuracy of predicted linkages:
Given the absence of a genome-wide gold standard for gene-to-peak linkages in the mouse
gastrula, we turned to external single-cell multiome datasets with matched, high-confidence
promoter-enhancer interaction data to benchmark performance. Specifically, we applied
BioCRE, Signac and ArchR to publicly available single-cell multiome data from human PBMC
cells and Gm12878 cells, using promoter-capture Hi-C (PCHiC) data as an orthogonal
reference for true regulatory interactions (Response Fig. R3j).
To enable a comprehensive and balanced evaluation, we defined both positive and negative
controls: positive linkages were inferred from PCHiC-confirmed interactions, while negative
linkages were established as peak-gene pairs showing no chromatin interactions within a 1 Mb
range in the PCHiC data. We evaluated the performance using multiple following metrics:
 The metrics of Macro-F1 score across all linkages showed that BioCRE consistently
achieved higher scores than both Signac and ArchR across all tested cell types, with strong
reproducibility across replicates (Response Fig. R3j-1). This indicates that BioCRE’s
predictions more closely align with the experimentally determined chromatin architecture.
 The Macro-F1 score for linkages of all three tools shared genes revealed that BioCRE
outperformed both Signac and ArchR in most cell types, where its advantage was less
pronounced (Response Fig. R3j-2).
 The True Positive Rate (TPR) for linkages unique to each method was also assessed.
BioCRE-specific linkages show comparable or higher level of TPR than those of Signac
and ArchR (Response Fig. R3j-3), suggesting that BioCRE-specific predictions are not
only robust but also biologically credible.
Thus, through incorporating external dataset and gold standard chromatin interaction dataset,
we demonstrated that BioCRE exhibits consistent superiority in linkage identification than
Signac and ArchR.
These results have been included in the revised manuscript (Line 162-176; Supplementary
Fig. 4), the detailed method has been provided in Line 982-1038, and we also acknowledged
the significance of systematically benchmark of BioCRE performance and discussed about the
current limitations in Line 623-632, Line 703-705.

BioCRE, Signac, and ArchR, respectively. c. Venn diagram showing the intersection of predicted gene-peak linkages.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, Yang and colleagues present a spatiotemporal dataset capturing mouse
gastrulation, generated using 10x Genomics Multiome data. The study involves a
significant amount of data integration and projection, incorporating external datasets such
as Geo-seq and ChIP-seq. To enable gene regulatory network (GRN) analysis, the authors
developed a new computational tool called BioCREs, which they claim performs better
than existing pipelines. They also adapted the Tangram algorithm—originally designed for
high-resolution spatial transcriptomics—for use with their data to align it with Geo-seq
references. Through this combined approach, they aim to map spatial and temporal
regulatory changes during gastrulation.
The scope of this work is impressive, and the integration of multiple data types is interesting.
The authors also acknowledge the limitations of current spatial resolution and mismatched
cell type references, which are important caveats. I appreciate the validation experiments
included, which lend support to some of their conclusions. That said, I do have several
concerns, especially regarding the BioCREs pipeline and the modified Tangram tool.
Response: We highly appreciate the reviewer’s positive assessment and constructive
suggestions on our manuscript. In this revision, we have carefully revised the manuscript,
especially for the benchmarking of BioCRE pipeline and comparing the ST-MAGIC results with
Stereo-seq results. Generally, these efforts further strengthen our results.
Major Concerns:
1. The claim that BioCREs outperforms Signac and ArchR is based on a single
performance index. This is insufficient to justify the claim. Benchmarking against
established regulatory element datasets (e.g., ENCODE) is necessary to validate accuracy
and specificity.
Response: Thanks for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree that a more comprehensive
benchmarking strategy is essential to substantiate our claim that BioCRE outperforms existing
tools.
In this revision, to systematically benchmark the performance of BioCRE, we have conducted
a series of systematic evaluations to rigorously compare the performance of BioCRE against
the state-of-the-art methods: Signac and ArchR.
1. The set characteristics of predicted gene-to-peak linkages:
Using our multi-omic dataset from the mouse gastrula, we evaluated the number, biological
relevance, and cell type specificity of predicted gene-to-peak linkages. As shown, BioCRE
identified 44,644 gene-to-peak linkages, with a median gene-to-peak distance of 127,175 bp
(Response Fig. R23a, b). Comparative analyses revealed that 28,472 linkages (64%) were
specifically identified in BioCRE (Response Fig. R23c, d). Gene ontology analyses of genes
associated with these BioCRE-specific linkages (28,472 linkages) revealed significant
enrichment in embryo development, including heart development, liver development, and
nervous system development (Response Fig. R23e). This result suggests that these BioCRE-
specific linkages could be responsible for the regulation of embryo development related genes.
To assess the cell type specificity of predicted linkages, we analyzed the accessibility of peaks
linked to cell type-specific genes identified by each tool (Response Fig. R23f, g). Using UMAP
visualization and quantifying clustering coherence with the Silhouette score, we found that
linkages predicted by BioCRE gets a higher score compared to those from Signac and ArchR,
indicating a more effective capability for BioCRE to capture cell type-specific linkages
(Response Fig. R23f, g).
Together, these results demonstrate that BioCRE could be adept at identify cell-type-specific
linkages, which are likely to play key roles in orchestrating embryo development.
2. The computational efficiency and robustness of predicting linkages:
We assessed the computational efficiency and robustness of different methods under varying
sampling conditions. Overall, we found that the built-in deep-learning bi-orientation regression
model for BioCRE does not incur excessive run-time costs, showing comparable performance
to ArchR (Response Fig. R23h). To evaluate the robustness of linkage identification, we
checked the consistency of predicted linkages across three distinct down-sampling scenarios:
 In the first scenario, where both RNA and peak reads were down-sampled concurrently,
BioCRE demonstrated the highest recovery rate of linkage identification (Response Fig.
R23i). To specify, 40.9% linkages (31,911 out of 78,109) are constantly identified in
BioCRE, while only 8.2% linkages (3,677 out of 44,705) for Signac and 5.7% linkages
(4,479 out of 79,067) for ArchR show consistent results among variable sample sizes
(Response Fig. R23i-1).
 In the second scenario, where only RNA reads were down-sampled while peak reads
remain unchanged, we found that 44.6% linkages (21,406 out of 48,043) are consistently
captured for BioCRE (Response Fig. R23i-2). In the meantime, 42.9% linkages (18,335
out of 42,937) for Signac and 61.9% linkages (38,510 out of 62,226) for ArchR are stably
identified (Response Fig. R23i-2).
 In the last scenario, we specifically down-sampled peak reads and then performed linkage
identification (Response Fig. R23i-3). Consequently, we found that 52.1% linkages
(49,476/95,042) for BioCRE are captured across all down-sampling groups (Response
Fig. R23i-3). In contrast, only 24.1% linkages (9,122/37,894) for Signac and 46.2%
linkages (28,388/61,422) for ArchR show the same pattern (Response Fig. R23i-3).
Collectively, these analyses demonstrate that BioCRE achieves a favorable balance between
computational efficiency and robustness, exhibiting consistently high reproducibility in linkage
prediction across diverse and reduced sequencing depths, particularly under conditions of
limited chromatin accessibility data (Scenario 1 and 3), highlighting its reliability in practical,
resource-variable setting.
3. The reliability and accuracy of gene-to-peak linkages:
Given the absence of a genome-wide gold standard for gene-to-peak linkages in the mouse
gastrula, we turned to external single-cell multiome datasets with matched, high-confidence
promoter-enhancer interaction data to benchmark performance. Specifically, we applied
BioCRE, Signac and ArchR to publicly available single-cell multiome data from human PBMC
cells and Gm12878 cells, using promoter-capture Hi-C (PCHiC) data as an orthogonal
reference for true regulatory interactions (Response Fig. R23j).
To enable a comprehensive and balanced evaluation, we defined both positive and negative
controls: positive linkages were inferred from PCHiC-confirmed interactions, while negative
linkages were established as peak-gene pairs showing no chromatin interactions within a 1 Mb
range in the PCHiC data. We evaluated the performance using multiple following metrics:
 The metrics of Macro-F1 score across all linkages showed that BioCRE consistently
achieved higher scores than both Signac and ArchR across all tested cell types, with strong
reproducibility across replicates (Response Fig. R23j-1). This indicates that BioCRE’s
predictions more closely align with the experimentally determined chromatin architecture.
 The Macro-F1 score for linkages of all three tools shared genes revealed that BioCRE
outperformed both Signac and ArchR in most cell types except in CD16 monocyte, , where
its advantage was less pronounced (Response Fig. R23j-2).
 The True Positive Rate (TPR) for linkages unique to each method was also assessed.
BioCRE-specific linkages show comparable or higher level of TPR than those of Signac
and ArchR (Response Fig. R23j-3), suggesting that BioCRE-specific predictions are not
only robust but also biologically credible.
Thus, through incorporating external dataset and gold standard chromatin interaction dataset,
we demonstrated that BioCRE exhibits consistent superiority in linkage identification than
Signac and ArchR.
These results have been included in the revised manuscript (Line 162-176; Supplementary
Fig. 4), the detailed method has been provided in Line 982-1038, and we also acknowledged
the significance of systematically benchmark of BioCRE performance and discussed about the
current limitations in Line 623-632, Line 703-705.
Response Figure R23. Benchmark of BioCRE. a. Bar plot showing the number of gene-peak linkages identified by
BioCRE, Signac, and ArchR. b. Histogram showing the median gene-peak distance for linkages identified by BioCRE,
Signac, and ArchR. c. Venn diagram showing the intersection of predicted gene-peak linkages. d. Bar plot highlighting
the ratio of non-overlapping linkage ratios for each tool. e. Gene ontology analyses for BioCRE-specific captured
linkages associated genes. f. UMAP visualization based on the chromatin accessibility of cell type-specific genes
associated peaks. g. Silhouette score evaluating the cell type distribution specificity. h. Line plot depicting the runtime
for each tool with variable proportion of reads. BioCRE was running on a single GPU (A100), while ArchR and Signac
were executed using 20 CPU cores for parallel computing, respectively. i. The effects of sequencing reads down-
sampling on linkage composition consistency for each tool. The constant linkage numbers for each scenario are
highlighted in red. j. The prediction and validation of gene-peak linkages using external multiome dataset and gold
standard promoter-enhancer interaction dataset.
2. Distal vs. Proximal regulatory region comparison: The comparison between "Distal High"
and "Proximal" groups is biased by excluding the "Distal Low" group. A more appropriate
comparison would be between all distal regions and proximal ones, with proper statistical
testing (e.g., p-values) to support conclusions.
Response: Thanks for your constructive suggestion. As recommended, we have directly
compared the JSS score between proximal and distal linked peaks—including both 'distal high'
and 'distal low' groups—thereby providing a more balanced and representative assessment.
Statistical testing (Wilcoxon rank-sum test) confirms that, on average, proximal peaks exhibit
significantly higher JSS scores than distal peaks (Response Fig. R24a), supporting their
stronger association with gene expression variation.
Additionally, we retained the comparison with the "distal high" group as a secondary analysis
to emphasize the particularly strong regulatory potential of this subset, clearly distinguishing it
from the broader distal category. We observed that a considerable number of distal linked
peaks exhibit higher JSS score than those of the proximal peaks (Response Fig. R24b),
highlighting the functional importance of certain distal regulatory elements during gastrulation.
These updated analyses have been incorporated into the Fig. 1f and Supplementary Fig. 5c.
Response Figure R24. Bar plots highlighting the JSS score measuring the consistency between gene
expression and linked peaks. a. The comparison between proximal and distal linked peaks. b. The distal peaks
were subdivided into distal high and distal low group based on the comparison with proximal peaks. Distal peaks were
annotated as peaks located outside TSS ± 2 kb, proximal peaks were annotated as peaks located within TSS ± 2 kb.
Wilcox tests were used to calculate the significances.
3. Insufficient benchmarking for BioCREs and modified Tangram: The manuscript lacks
technical detail and performance benchmarking for both pipelines. More rigorous testing is
needed to demonstrate their robustness and reliability.
Response: Thanks for raising this important issue. We are deeply sorry that the initial
submission lacked sufficient technical details and comprehensive benchmarking.
Regarding BioCRE, we have now conducted an extensive performance evaluation, as detailed
in our response to comment #1 and illustrated in Response Figure R23. This includes
comparisons with established methods—Signac and ArchR—across multiple metrics such as
cell type specificity (Silhouette score), computational efficiency, robustness to various sampling
depth, and accuracy against orthogonal chromatin interaction data (Macro-F1 and TPR scores).
The results consistently demonstrate that BioCRE, built on a bidirectional regression framework,
outperforms the other tools in key aspects relevant to gene-to-peak linkage prediction in
developmental contexts. These analyses have been integrated into the revised manuscript
(Line 162-176; Supplementary Fig. 4) to enhance methodological transparency and rigor.
With respect to the use of Tangram for spatiotemporal mapping, we clarify that our approach
does not involve fundamental modification to the Tangram algorithm itself. Instead, we have
adopted a more refined and biologically informed input strategy, as recommended in the official
Tangram documentation (https://github.com/broadinstitute/Tangram). The refinement strategy
of gene selection for Tangram has been benchmarked in a recent study15. Specifically, rather
than using all genes shared between the Geo-seq and 10x scMultiome datasets, we selected
stage-specific "zipcode" genes — those showing spatially restricted expression patterns during
gastrulation — to improve mapping accuracy. This refinement aligns with best practices and
enhances the biological relevance of the spatial inference (Supplementary Fig. 6c-i). We are
sorry that this aspect was not clearly described in the original submission. We have now
provided the complete list of genes used (Supplementary Table 2) and updated the method
with a detailed and accurate description of using tangram (Line 859-881).
4. Incorporating data from high-resolution platforms such as Visium HD or Stereo-seq
would significantly strengthen the spatial claims.
Response: Thanks for the valuable suggestion. We fully agree that incorporating high-
resolution spatial data, such as Visium HD or Stereo-seq, would strengthen the spatial claims
of the current study.
In this revision, we have incorporated a recently published Stereo-seq dataset (SEU-3D)16
covering the mouse early organogenesis embryos, to which we contributed, for direct
comparison with our ST-MAGIC atlas. As shown, to check the consistency of spatial results
between these two datasets (SEU-3D and ST-MAGIC), we first spatial-temporally aligned the
two datasets, then determined the transcriptional correlation of cell types and spatial
concordance of cell type marker geneset (CTGs) expression, and finally checked the
reproducibility of key spatial findings reported in the current study (Response Fig. R25a).
Generally, spatial transcriptomic data from the E7.5 stage were used, the spatial coordinate
along z-axis (proximal-distal axis) and the cell types annotated in both datasets were aligned
according to their respective sampling strategies (Response Fig. R25b). Pearson correlation
analyses of cell type transcriptome reported that most cell types were well correlated
(Response Fig. R25c). Moreover, the spatial distribution of CTGs were also highly consistent
(Response Fig. R25d). We first present the AUC scores of the top 500 marker gene sets for
each cell types (illustrated for VE, SE, and CE) in SEU-3D, where the spatial distribution of
these scores aligns well with the known anatomical localization of each cell type (first column).
Applying the identical analytical to ST-MAGIC reveals a highly similar spatial pattern (second
column), demonstrating the consistency of marker gene enrichment across reconstruction
methods. To enable a more granular comparison, we then performed a layer-by-layer analysis
relative to Stereo-seq and GEO-seq. For each cell type, we extracted corresponding single-cell
profiles from Stereo-seq and matched them with spot-level single-cell compositions in each
layer of GEO-seq. The similarity between these matched cell populations was assessed using
the marker gene sets. As shown in the results, high similarity is observed at spatially
corresponding locations (third column), while gray regions indicate positions where data were
not jointly present in both datasets. For example, the expression of marker geneset for visceral
endoderm cells were highly enriched in outer layer cells of SEU-3D map and in EA and EP
regions of the ST-MAGIC atlas (Response Fig. R25d). Spatial correlation analysis confirmed
that this enrichment is anatomically coherent, as expression of these markers correlates
obviously only in regions where visceral endoderm is known to reside (Response Fig. R25d).
Then, we checked the spatial distribution of specific cell types and genes between SEU-3D and
ST-MAGIC atlas. As shown in Response Fig. R25e (Fig. 2b in the manuscript), mesenchyme
cells were located at the proximal posterior region and paraxial mesoderm 1 cells were
distributed at the anterior medial mesoderm region according to both ST-MAGIC atlas and
experimental results (Fig. 2b, c). Here, we found that mesenchyme and paraxial mesoderm
cells exhibit similar spatial patterns in SEU-3D atlas. Furthermore, the expression patterns of
canonical markers such as Hand1 (mesenchyme) and Irx5 (paraxial mesoderm) align closely
between the two platforms, further corroborating the accuracy of our ST-MAGIC atlas.
We acknowledge that direct integration is challenged by inherent technical differences: SEU-
3D achieves near single cell bin resolution but with lower transcriptomic depth (~400–600
genes per bin), whereas ST-MAGIC spots capture richer molecular profiles (~3,500–4,500

### Reviewer 1

The authors have improved the manuscript and addressed many of my comments. I commend the authors again for including many data panels that make it possible to evaluate the data and claims. Nonetheless, I have some remaining concerns.

Figure 1:
Please include the number of embryos into the table in ED Fig 1e. I’m surprised that the number of cells in each embryo included in this study is not available and a literature based reference is given, especially because 10x genomics recommends loading numbers as part of the protocol. I appreciate that a reference number is included now as I believe it is important to assess sampling.

ED Fig 3a: From my understanding of the authors’ response, I believe that ED Fig 3a is mislabeled as it does not represent differential gene expression (DEG). Differential gene expression is an analysis where two or more groups are compared against each other. From the description, I believe that ED Fig 3a is Cell type-specific genes and ED Fig 3b is Cell type-specific accessible peaks. It is not clear from the manuscript how these genes are selected, which could be from DEG analysis. The Methods state “marker genes specific to each cell type were mainly used to annotate clusters…” but it is not stated how the marker genes were identified. My apologies if I missed it. Will the authors please explain how the genes in ED Fig 3 are selected?

BioCRE:
The authors use GO analysis to show that BioCRE-specific linkages are enriched in embryo development. Since the purpose of the analysis is to benchmark against the other methods, would the authors please also show the GO analysis results for Signac and ArchR?

The downsampling analysis revealed interesting behavior from BioCRE. In Scenario 1, BioCRE returns approximately the same number of linkages for all of the downsampled sets, with a trend where more data leads to a smaller set. This is in contrast to Signac and ArchR which show an increased set size with increased data input. Scenarios 2 and 3 show that this difference in behavior is driven by the ATAC-seq data. The behavior, to me, implies that Signac and ArchR are prioritizing precision while BioCRE prioritizes recall. The desire to prioritize precision is sometimes preferred due to the need to prioritize targets for experimental validation.

The next analysis seeks to assess the tools against a gold standard. Will the authors please show the results in terms of precision and recall rather than the combined Macro-F1 score? Moreover, it is not clear to me why results are shown relative to BioCRE’s scores rather than, for example, showing each tool’s precision score. Given my comment above, I am curious how precision and recall behave for the downsampled data sets.

Figure 5.
I appreciate that the authors included a panel showing the enrichment of cells that are Shh+, Noto+, Foxj1+ (ED F14c). Indeed, it does look enriched in the position of the node. Nonetheless, I do not believe the new plots are sufficient to support their claim that there are two distinct subtypes (Shh+Noto-Foxj1- and Shh+Noto+Foxj1+). From the scRNA-seq data, what proportion of the cells fall into these two categories. Presumably they form two subclusters if the authors are confident in defining the subtypes. Is there a plot they can provide to support this claim?

Fig 5l. I believe the authors mean “specific expression” and not “specific distribution”

Figure 6.
Thank you for changing the wording in the manuscript to better match the figure panel. Given the complexity about the dynamics of the system, I believe it will be worthwhile to include a quantitative figure panel better illustrating the temporal dynamics of the regulation. Can the authors please include bar plots or line plots?

### Reviewer 2

I am satisfied with the revised version.
